parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the later part of the curve in Fig. 2.1 where the velocity stops increasing and becomes flat - what does that flat level tell you about the forces and the velocity?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot When Velocity Stops Changing**
Terminal velocity is reached when drag balances weight so there is no resultant force and velocity stays constant. On a $v$-$t$ graph that looks like the curve levelling off to become horizontal.

Step 2: **Read Off the Flat Value**
In Fig. 2.1 the curve flattens from about $t = 20\text{ s}$ onwards at: $$v = 39\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is the terminal velocity.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: acceleration as gradient of v-t graph
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the steepness of a velocity-time graph represents at any instant, and why you need to touch the curve at only one point at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$ to find it.
Hint 2: Once your line is drawn, pick two widely spaced points on that straight line itself (not on the curve) and use their $v$ and $t$ values to work out its steepness.
parts.proper_answer: Draw tangent to curve at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$; $a =$ gradient $= \Delta v / \Delta t \approx 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$ (allow $0.9$ to $1.1\text{ m s}^{-2}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Gradient for Instantaneous Acceleration**
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. On a $v$-$t$ graph: $$a = \text{gradient of } v\text{-}t \text{ graph}$$ Because the graph is curved, acceleration is changing, so you need the gradient exactly at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$. That means drawing a tangent - a straight line that just touches the curve at that point and follows its slope.

Step 2: **Draw Tangent and Calculate Gradient**
Draw a good tangent at $t = 9.0\text{ s}$ extending over a large $t$-range to reduce uncertainty. Then calculate: $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ For example, using points on the tangent such as $(0, 26\text{ m s}^{-1})$ and $(18\text{ s}, 44\text{ m s}^{-1})$: $$a = \frac{44 - 26}{18 - 0} \approx 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ Any well-drawn tangent gives $0.9$ to $1.1\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing the two vertical forces at time $t_1$ - which one pulls down and which one pushes up, and which is larger just after the parachute opens?
Hint 2: Work out the size of the downward pull due to gravity from the given mass before you combine anything.
Hint 3: Think about how to combine an upward force and a downward force to get the resultant force, taking care with positive and negative signs.
Hint 4: Recall how resultant force is linked to mass and acceleration for working out the acceleration from your resultant force.
Hint 5: Check the sign of your answer to decide whether the acceleration points in the same direction as the fall or opposite to it.
parts.proper_answer: Weight $= 68 \times 9.81 = 667\text{ N}$ downwards, drag $= 1800\text{ N}$ upwards. Resultant $F \approx -1130\text{ N}$, $a = F/m \approx -17\text{ m s}^{-2}$, so magnitude $17\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards (opposite to motion).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the Two Forces**
Take downwards as positive for the calculation. Weight always acts downwards: $$W = mg$$ Drag from the parachute acts upwards, opposing motion. Just after opening, drag $= 1800\text{ N}$ is much larger than weight, so the resultant will be upwards and the skydiver will decelerate.

Step 3: **Find Resultant Force**
Upward is negative if downwards is positive: $$(\Sigma)F = W - \text{drag}$$ $$(\Sigma)F = 68 \times 9.81 - 1800 \approx 667 - 1800 \approx -1133\text{ N}$$ The minus sign means the net force is about $1130\text{ N}$ upwards.

Step 4: **Apply Newton's Second Law**
$$a = \frac{(\Sigma)F}{m}$$ $$a = \frac{-1133}{68} \approx -17\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Step 5: **Give Magnitude and Direction**
Magnitude is $17\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to 2 s.f. The negative sign means direction is opposite to velocity, i.e. upwards. This large upward acceleration rapidly slows the fall.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what momentum depends on, and what the starting velocity at $t_1$ and the finishing velocity at $t_3$ are for this slowing-down interval.
Hint 2: Remember you can factor out the constant mass and just multiply it by the overall change in velocity, keeping the sign to show a decrease.
parts.proper_answer: $\Delta p = m(v - u) = 68 \times (5.7 - 39) \approx -2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$, i.e. a decrease of $2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Change in Momentum**
Momentum is $p = mv$. Mass stays at $68\text{ kg}$. At $t_1$ velocity is the first terminal velocity $u = 39\text{ m s}^{-1}$ downwards. At $t_3$ velocity is $v = 5.7\text{ m s}^{-1}$ downwards. Change is final minus initial: $$\Delta p = mv - mu = m(v - u)$$

Step 2: **Substitute and Calculate**
$$\Delta p = 68 \times (5.7 - 39)$$ $$\Delta p = 68 \times (-33.3) \approx -2.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ N s}$$ The negative sign shows momentum decreases in the downward direction. Magnitude of change is about $2300\text{ N s}$.
